scenes.title: The Short Weight
scenes.text:
The Salt House kept its ledgers on the third floor, under the eaves, where the damp could not reach them and the clerks could not reach anything else. Ilse Varga had worked there for four years and had never once been warm.

She sat at the long table with the Kestrel's book open in front of her and the Kestrel's tally-sticks laid out beside it in a row, like the bones of a small animal. Every sack that went over the side of a salt-ship at Varrow was notched on a stick by the pan-reeve and notched again by the ship's mate, and the stick was split down its length so that each man kept half. When the halves came back to the Salt House they were matched, and counted, and the count went into the book. It was the oldest honest thing in the city. Nobody could cut a notch out of a stick without the other half showing it.

She counted the sticks again. Thirty-four sticks, ten notches to a stick. Three hundred and forty measures.

The book said four hundred.

"You're frowning at it," said Aurek Stiles from the far end of the table. He was the senior of the three tallyclerks and had been for twenty years, and he said it without looking up from his own work. "Frowning at a ledger is how the ink gets into your face."

"The Kestrel," Ilse said. "Her book says four hundred measures out on the ninth. I've got three hundred and forty on the sticks."

"Then you've dropped six sticks behind the stove."

"I haven't."

"Then the mate's dropped them in the harbour. It happens." Aurek turned a page. "Write it as received and put a query in the margin. The Magister reads the margins."

She did not write it as received. She sat with the pen over the page until the ink beaded on the nib and fell, a small black star on the blotter, and then she got up and went down the narrow stair to the Magister's room.

Magister Oduya Fenn had run the Salt House since before Ilse was born. He was a tall man gone thin in the way of tall men who forget to eat, and his room was the only warm one in the building, because he had the only good stove. He looked up when she knocked and smiled at her with real pleasure, which made what she had come to say harder.

"Ilse. Sit. You look like you've been out on the Pans."

"Only on the third floor, Magister." She did not sit. "The Kestrel's book is sixty measures over her sticks."

The smile stayed exactly where it was. That was the first thing she would remember afterward — not that it went, but that it stayed, a little too long, like a man holding a door that nobody was coming through.

"Sixty," he said.

"Six sticks. I've counted three times."

"The Kestrel came in through the Gullet in a rising sea. Her mate was sick over the side twice before they'd cleared the bar — your brother will tell you, he took her in." Fenn spread his long hands. "Sticks go missing. The book is written from the manifest at the pans, and the manifest is right."

"Then the sticks should be with the manifest."

"Then they should." He said it kindly. "Write the book as it stands, Ilse. I'll speak to the pan-reeve myself."

She went back up the stairs. Aurek did not ask her what had been said, and she did not tell him. She wrote four hundred in the column in her own clean hand, and in the margin she wrote nothing at all, because the Magister read the margins.

When the bell went for the end of the day she put the thirty-four sticks into her satchel instead of into the bin. She did not decide to do it. Her hands did it while she was thinking about something else, and by the time she noticed, she was already on the stair.

scenes.title: The Quay at Low Water
scenes.text:
Varrow at low water smelt of mud and iron and the sweet rot of weed, and the whole of the lower town came down to the quay to look at the sky.

There was a storm coming. Ilse could see it from the top of the Gull Stair, a long bruise lying along the horizon to the south-west, with the light behind it gone the colour of a boiled sweet. The harbour had drained down to its channels and the salt-ships sat over on their bilges in the mud, masts leaning together like drunk men holding each other up. Below her the stair went down in its two hundred worn steps to the quay, and the quay was full.

She found Tomas where she always found him, sitting on an upturned basket outside the pilots' shed with a pipe he never lit, looking at the water as if it owed him money.

"You took the Kestrel in," she said.

"Hello, Ilse. Good day at the counting? Lovely to see you, Tomas." He moved over on the basket to make room for her. "I took her in on the ninth. Why?"

"Was it rough?"

"It was the Gullet in a southerly. It's always rough." He looked at her properly. Her brother was three years older than her and had their mother's face, broad and patient, and the same habit of knowing what she was going to say before she said it and waiting for her to say it anyway. "What's wrong with the Kestrel?"

"Was her mate sick?"

Tomas laughed. "Jory Pell? Jory's been at sea since he could walk. He's never been sick in his life. He was singing." He stopped laughing. "Why?"

She told him. She kept her voice down, though nobody on the quay was listening to anything but the wind getting up. Tomas listened with the pipe in his teeth.

"Sixty measures," he said at last. "That's — what is that, in silver?"

"At the Hesk price, nine hundred crowns. Near enough."

He whistled, low. "And the Magister said."

"He said sticks go missing."

"They do." But he was frowning now, the way she must have been frowning at the ledger. "Not six of them off one ship, they don't. A man might lose one. Six is a decision." He took the pipe out of his mouth and turned it over. "What are you going to do?"

"I don't know. I wrote it in. Four hundred."

"Ilse."

"What was I supposed to write? He's the Magister. He got me the place." She pressed the satchel against her side and felt the sticks shift inside it. "I took the sticks."

Tomas looked at the satchel and then at her. "You took the — that's the Salt House's property."

"I know what it is."

"If anybody knew they were short, they'll know you took them."

"Nobody knows they were short. Aurek thinks I dropped them behind the stove."

The first of the rain came then, a few fat drops striking the stones between their feet, each one leaving a dark coin. All along the quay people began to move, hauling covers over baskets, shouting for children. Out past the harbour mouth the sea had gone a hard, flat grey.

"Go home," Tomas said. "Put them somewhere dry. Don't do anything else tonight." He stood up and knocked the pipe against his palm out of habit, though there was nothing in it. "I've got to see to the Patience before this comes in. I'll come by tomorrow."

"Tomas —"

"Tomorrow." He put a hand on her head, the way he had when she was small, and then he was gone into the crowd, a broad back in an oilskin, moving against the people coming up.

She climbed the Gull Stair in the rain. By the time she reached the top the storm had come in over the bar and the whole harbour was white.

scenes.title: A Letter Under the Door
scenes.text:
Her room was over the cooper's, at the top of a house so narrow that the stair went up through the middle of it like the stone in a plum. She lit the lamp and put the sticks on the table and looked at them for a while, and then she put them inside the hollow of the bolster, which was the only hiding place she had, and felt foolish.

The rain beat on the slates. Somewhere below her the cooper's wife was singing to the baby, the same three lines over and over.

It was close to midnight when someone knocked.

She did not open the door. She stood behind it with the lamp in one hand and the poker in the other and said, "Who is it?"

"A friend of your brother's," said a man's voice. It was light and pleasant and not from Varrow — there was something of the capital in the vowels, or something trying to sound like it. "Though I doubt he'd put it that way. Please don't hit me with whatever you're holding."

"What do you want?"

"To give you something. You can open the door a hand's width and I'll put it through, and then I'll go away, and you'll never have to look at me." A pause. "Though I'm told I'm not bad to look at."

She opened the door a hand's width. The man on the landing was perhaps thirty, soaked through, his dark hair plastered to his skull. He had a long, clever face and a scar through one eyebrow and he was smiling as if this were all a great joke that she would be let in on presently.

He held out a packet wrapped in oilcloth.

"What is it?"

"A letter. Not to you. I think you'd better have it anyway." He kept holding it out. "My name's Corin Ashe. Your brother knows me. He'll tell you I'm a liar and a smuggler, and he'll be right about the second one."

"Why would you give me a letter that isn't to me?"

"Because I can read, Miss Varga, and having read it I'd rather it were in the hands of someone who counts sticks than in mine." He pushed the packet through the gap. She took it, mostly to stop him dropping it. It was heavier than a letter ought to be. "There's a seal on it you'll recognise. Don't break it here. Don't break it at all, if you've any sense. Just — keep it somewhere."

"How do you know about the sticks?"

But he had already turned. She heard him going down the stair, light and quick, missing the step that creaked as if he knew it was there. The street door opened and shut.

She closed her own door and bolted it and set the lamp down and turned the packet over in her hands. Under the oilcloth was good paper, folded small, and a seal of red wax pressed with a ship under a crown.

It was the seal of the Harbour Reeve.

Ilse sat on the bed with the letter in her lap and the sticks in the bolster under her and listened to the rain until the lamp burned down.

scenes.title: The Reeve's Seal
scenes.text:
She broke the seal in the morning, of course. Corin Ashe had known she would; that was why he had told her not to.

The storm had blown itself out in the night and left the sky scoured and pale. She sat at her table with a heel of yesterday's bread and slid the blade of her knife under the wax, carefully, so that it lifted in one piece and she could have pressed it back if she had been a different sort of person. Inside was a single sheet, folded twice, in a secretary's hand. At the bottom, a signature she had seen on a hundred harbour warrants. Halvard Seyle, Reeve of Varrow.

The letter was to Fenn.

_Magister —_

_The sixty from the Kestrel will go with the rest. The Black Mare lies off the Chapel on the spring tide and will take all of it then; there is no other night. Ormund leaves the capital on the twelfth and will be with you within the week, so see that the books are clean before she comes. I need not tell you what a clean book means. The levy is paid in full this year, as every year. You have my word on the Pans._

_— H.S._

She read it four times. The fourth time she read it aloud, very quietly, to hear whether it said something else when it was spoken. It did not.

_The sixty from the Kestrel._ So it was not six sticks dropped in the harbour. _With the rest._ So it was not only the Kestrel. She thought of all the books on the third floor, the forty years of them on their shelves under the eaves, and of how many times she had written a number into a column without counting the sticks, because the sticks had been counted by somebody else, because the Magister read the margins.

_You have my word on the Pans._ That one she did not understand at all.

She folded the letter again and looked at the seal, and then she did a thing she was not proud of: she warmed the knife over the lamp and pressed the wax back down, so that from a little way off it looked whole. Then she put the letter inside her bodice, against her skin, where it crackled when she breathed, and she went to work.

Aurek Stiles was already at the long table. He looked up when she came in and said, "You look like a woman who's slept on a bag of nails," and she said, "I found the sticks," and he said, "Behind the stove?" and she said, "Behind the stove," and took them out of her satchel and put them in the bin, all thirty-four.

It was the first lie she had told at the Salt House. It went down easier than she had expected, and that frightened her more than the letter did.

At midday she went down to the Magister's room on an errand about the Heron's book and stood in his doorway while he signed it. His hand did not shake. He asked after Tomas, and whether the Patience had come through the storm, and he told her she was the best clerk he had had in thirty years, which he had told her before. She watched him sign and thought: _see that the books are clean._

She had always believed that she could tell when someone was lying to her. She went back up the stairs knowing that she had been wrong about that, and did not know for how long.

scenes.title: The Auditor
scenes.text:
The auditor came two days early.

Ilse heard her before she saw her — a carriage on the cobbles of Tallow Street, which was a thing that did not happen; nobody drove a carriage into the lower town because the streets were too narrow and the carters too rude. Then voices in the yard, and the porter's voice going up high the way it did when he was frightened, and then a long silence, and then feet on the stair.

Lisbet Ormund was not what Ilse had expected. She had pictured someone like the Magister, tall and grey and sorrowful, or someone like the Reeve, red-faced and loud. The woman who came into the third-floor room was small and round and perhaps fifty, in a brown travelling coat with the mud of the coast road still on its hem, and she had a face like a kindly hen. She stood in the doorway and looked at the shelves of ledgers, all forty years of them, with an expression of pure delight.

"Oh," she said. "Oh, look at that. You keep them up here? Under the roof?"

"It's the driest room, madam," said Aurek, who had got to his feet so fast his stool had gone over.

"It's the hottest room in summer," said Lisbet Ormund. "Paper doesn't like heat any more than it likes damp. Never mind. Never mind." She came in and took off her gloves. "I'm the Exchequer's auditor. I expect you've been told I'd be along. I expect you were told the twentieth." She smiled at both of them. "I find it saves a great deal of everyone's time to come on the eighteenth."

Ilse found that she had stood up too, and that her hand had gone flat against the front of her bodice, where the letter was. She took it away.

"Magister Fenn —" Aurek began.

"Is downstairs, and has given me the run of the place, and very gracious he was about it. He's sending up tea. You'll be Master Stiles. And you are —?"

"Ilse Varga, madam. Tallyclerk."

"Varga." The auditor looked at her a moment longer than was comfortable. "There was a Varga at the Hesk customs house, years ago. A woman. Very good with figures."

"My mother, madam."

"Was she? Well." Lisbet Ormund turned back to the shelves. "Then you'll know the difference between a book that's right and a book that's tidy, Miss Varga. Most people don't." She ran a finger along the spines, the newest first. "I'll want this year's, and last year's, and — let me see — the year of the big tide. When was that? Three years back?"

"Four, madam," said Aurek.

"Three," said Ilse, at the same moment.

They looked at each other. The auditor looked at both of them, pleasantly.

"The spring tide that took the Pans," Ilse said. "It was three years in Thawmonth. I'd been here a year."

"Then I'll have that one," said Lisbet Ormund, "and the one before it, so I can see the difference. And I'll have the tally-sticks for whatever's come in this month. All of them." She sat down at the end of the long table, in the place where nobody ever sat because the draught came under the door there, and folded her small hands. "I'm told sticks go missing," she said. "I'm told it happens all the time."

Nobody said anything. Down in the yard the porter was shouting for someone to bring up the tea.

That night Ilse did not go home over the cooper's. She went down the Gull Stair to the quay, and she did not find Tomas on his basket outside the pilots' shed, and when she asked old Mother Gannet, who sold eels at the foot of the stair and saw everything, the old woman only said that the Patience had gone out on the evening ebb, and that there'd been two men in her, and that one of them was a long clever one with a scar in his eyebrow.

scenes.title: Night Work
scenes.text:
The Patience was a pilot's boat, broad in the beam and built for the Gullet, and she did not like being asked to go quietly. Every block on her creaked; the mast talked to itself; the bilge-water slopped from side to side like a fat man laughing. Tomas Brenn had sailed her for eleven years and had never once wanted her to be quiet before.

"You could oil something," said Corin Ashe from the bow.

"You could shut up."

"I could." Corin was lying back against the anchor-warp with his hands behind his head, looking at the stars, as if he had been brought out here for the air. "I won't, though. I talk when I'm nervous. Everyone has something."

"You don't look nervous."

"That's the trick of it."

They had come out on the ebb at dusk, through the harbour mouth and then hard to starboard into the marsh channels, where the Salt House had its Pans and nobody else had any reason to go. The tide was making now. Tomas could feel it through the tiller, the water beginning to push up the channels from the sea, filling the little creeks one by one. In two hours there would be enough water over the Chapel bar for something bigger than the Patience to come in. That was what Corin had told him. That was what the forty crowns in his coat pocket were for.

"I'm not carrying anything," Tomas said. "You said that. Nothing in the boat."

"Nothing in the boat. We're going to look. That's all. You know the channels and I don't, and I want to see a thing with my own eyes before I say I've seen it." Corin turned his head. "Your sister's got the letter."

Tomas nearly put them on the mud. "You gave it to her."

"Somebody had to have it, and it couldn't be me. I'm not the sort of man people believe."

"She's a clerk. She's — she's got a room over the cooper's and a place at the Salt House and that's all she's got. If the Reeve finds out —"

"Then he'll find out that a clerk at the Salt House has a letter in his hand saying he's robbing the Exchequer," said Corin. "And then he'll have to decide what to do about her, in front of an auditor. Which is a great deal harder than deciding what to do about me in a dark alley." He was quiet a moment. "I'm sorry. I didn't think she'd be in it this long. I thought she'd take it straight to the auditor and the auditor would take it straight to the capital and that would be that."

"You don't know Ilse."

"I'm learning."

The channel opened out. Ahead of them, black against the stars, rose the broken tower of the Drowned Chapel, which had stood on an island in the marsh once, before the sea moved, and now stood up to its knees in the tide twice a day. Tomas let the sail down and they drifted, the Patience turning slowly on the flood.

There was a light at the Chapel.

Not a lantern — a shielded thing, a slit of yellow, low down near the water. And past the Chapel, out where the channel met the sea, a shape that did not belong to the marsh: a hull, long and low, with two masts and no lights at all.

"The Black Mare," Corin said softly. All the laughter had gone out of his voice. "She's early."

"How early?"

"A night. A whole night." He sat up. "The letter said the spring tide. That's tomorrow."

Out at the Chapel the light moved. Tomas heard, very faint across the water, the knock of a boat against stone, and a man's voice, and the long dragging sound of something heavy being hauled over a gunwale.

"Salt," said Corin. "They're loading."

"We should go."

"We should." But Corin did not move. He was leaning forward, staring, his clever face gone still. "Tomas. There's a boat at the Chapel steps. Can you see whose?"

Tomas could. He had known her the moment the light swung across her stern, because he had taken her in through the Gullet on the ninth.

It was the Kestrel's longboat.

scenes.title: Mother Gannet
scenes.text:
Tomas did not come by the next day, as he had said he would, and he did not come the day after.

On the second morning Ilse went down the Gull Stair before the Salt House bell and found Mother Gannet already at her place at the foot of it, gutting eels into a bucket with a short black knife. The old woman had sold eels at the bottom of the stair for as long as there had been a stair, by her own account, and possibly longer. She had one eye milky and one eye sharp, and it was generally understood in the lower town that the milky one saw more.

"He's not back," Mother Gannet said, before Ilse had opened her mouth. "The Patience isn't on her mooring. I've had the boy up and down the quay since first light asking."

"Which boy?"

"Mine." The old woman jerked her chin. Sitting on the bottom step, eating a cold potato with great concentration, was a child of nine or ten in a man's coat cut down at the sleeves. He had a face so dirty it was hard to say whether he was a boy at all. "Wren. He runs for me. He's not mine, but he runs for me."

"Nobody's seen her," Wren said, through potato. "Not in the harbour. Not at the Pans. Tad Mossop says he saw a sail in the channels last night past the Heron Creek, but Tad Mossop says a lot of things."

Ilse sat down on the step beside him because her legs had decided it for her.

"He's a pilot," Mother Gannet said, not unkindly. "He knows every inch of that marsh. If he's out there he's out there because he means to be." She dropped an eel into the bucket. "Question is who he's out there with."

"Corin Ashe."

"Ah." The old woman's sharp eye went to her. "Then the question's what he's out there for."

Ilse looked at the bucket of eels, at the grey light on the mud, at the salt-ships still lying over on their sides from the ebb. She thought about the letter against her skin and about the auditor at the end of the long table in the draught, asking for the year of the big tide.

"Mother," she said. "You remember the tide that took the Pans."

"I remember every tide since the old king died."

"What happened after? To the Pans?"

Mother Gannet wiped the black knife on her apron and was quiet for long enough that Wren stopped chewing.

"Sea came over the wall at the spring tide in Thawmonth," she said at last. "Took the wall, took the pans behind it, took the pan-reeve's house and the pan-reeve's wife with it. Half the salt-works in Varrow, gone under in one night. The Salt House wrote to the capital for money to build it back, and the capital wrote back and said it was a matter for the harbour." She spat, neatly, into the mud. "So it was the Reeve's to mend, and the Reeve said there was no money for it, and for a whole year the pan-men sat on the quay with their hands in their laps. And then one day there was money. And the wall went up, and the pans went back, and everyone said what a fine man the Reeve was."

"Where did the money come from?"

"Nobody asked. That's the thing about money that comes when you need it. Nobody asks." The old woman picked up another eel. "Your mother would've asked."

"My mother's dead."

"So she is. And so's the pan-reeve's wife, and the Salt House is still standing, and the Reeve's still got his fine house on the hill, and his fine new wall, which I'll tell you for nothing is built of the worst stone I ever saw and won't see out another ten years of tides." The knife went in. "You asked."

Ilse stood up. "If Tomas comes back —"

"The boy'll find you." Mother Gannet did not look up. "Go to your counting, girl. Count something."

scenes.title: The Year of the Big Tide
scenes.text:
The ledger for the year of the big tide was bound in green, because the binder had run out of brown that winter, and it stood out on the shelf like a wrong note. Lisbet Ormund had it open on the long table when Ilse came up the stair, and beside it the book for the year before, bound in brown, and beside that a sheet of her own paper covered in tiny, very neat figures.

Aurek was not at his place. The auditor saw her looking.

"I've sent Master Stiles to the pan-reeve with a list of questions," she said. "It'll take him most of the day, I'm afraid, because the pan-reeve won't know the answers and will have to send to the Reeve's office for them. Sit down, Miss Varga. Sit there, where I can see you."

Ilse sat.

"I want to show you something," said the auditor, "and then I want to ask you something, and I'd like you to think before you answer the second thing, because I shall know if you don't." She turned the green ledger round. "This is Thawmonth, the year of the tide. Here — the week of the flood. Nothing comes in at all, which is what you'd expect. Here, the month after. Very little. Here, the month after that. And here," she turned a page, "is the first month that the books are short against the Hesk price."

Ilse looked. It was a column of numbers in Aurek's hand, tidy and upright, and beside each a ship's name and a date. There was nothing wrong with any of them.

"They're not short," she said.

"Not in the book. In the book they're very well. But I have here," the auditor tapped her own sheet, "every cargo of Varrow salt that was sold at Hesk that month, from the Hesk customs ledgers, which I had copied before I left the capital. And the Hesk ledgers say that Varrow sent them a good deal less salt than Varrow's books say it sent. About one part in seven less." She sat back. "One part in seven. Every month since. Three years."

One part in seven. Sixty measures out of four hundred was a little more than that. Ilse kept her face very still and felt the paper crackle under her bodice when she breathed.

"Somebody," said Lisbet Ormund, "is selling one-seventh of the salt of Varrow somewhere other than Hesk, and the books of the Salt House are written as though they weren't. Now. Here's my question." She leaned forward. "I don't think you're a thief, Miss Varga. I knew your mother. I don't think the Magister is a thief either, not in his heart, though I've been wrong about men's hearts before. But somebody in this building writes the numbers, and somebody tells them which numbers to write. Has anybody ever told you to write a number you knew was wrong?"

She thought about the Kestrel's book. Four hundred in her own clean hand.

She thought about Tomas, who had not come home.

She thought: _if I say yes, she'll ask who. And if I say who, they'll know it was me. And Tomas is somewhere out in the marsh, and I don't know where, and I don't know who else knows._

"No, madam," she said.

The auditor looked at her for a long moment. Then she nodded, slowly, and turned the green book back around, and picked up her pen.

"I'll be here until the spring tide," she said, without looking up. "After that I go back to the capital and write my report with whatever I have. If you think of anything before then, Miss Varga, I'd be very grateful to hear it. I'm at the Anchor, on Rope Walk. Anyone can tell you where it is."

Ilse went back to her own place and opened the Heron's book and could not see a single number in it.

scenes.title: What the Kestrel Carried
scenes.text:
They had been seen. Tomas never knew how — a turn of the Patience's sail against the sky, perhaps, or the creak of her blocks across still water, or simply that a man on the Chapel steps had looked up at the wrong moment. But the light at the Chapel went out all at once, and in the dark there was a shout, and then the sound of oars.

"Go," said Corin. "Go, go —"

Tomas went. He put the helm over and got the sail up in one long heave and the Patience came round, slow, so slow, broad-beamed old cow that she was, and the flood was against them now, pushing them back up toward the Chapel. Behind them the oars were coming on. Four oars at least. A longboat, light and fast, and the men in her knew the channel nearly as well as he did.

"They'll have us before the Heron Creek," Corin said.

"They won't."

"They will. I can count, Tomas, it's the only thing I'm good for besides lying." Corin was pulling off his boots. "There's a cut on the left — the one with the dead tree. Where does it go?"

"Nowhere. Mud. It's a dead end."

"Can a man stand in it?"

"At this tide? To his chest, maybe. What are you —"

"They want the boat. They'll follow the boat." Corin was on the gunwale now, crouched, his clever face white in the starlight. "And they want me more than they want you, because I'm the one they've been paying. So when I go over, you keep going, and you make a great deal of noise, and I'll make rather less." He grinned suddenly. "Tell your sister to keep the letter. Tell her it's worth more than I am."

"Corin —"

He went over the side without a splash. Tomas never heard him hit the water. One moment there was a man on the gunwale and the next there was the dark and the dead tree going past on the left and nothing else.

He kept going. He did not know what else to do. He made, as instructed, a great deal of noise — he let the mainsheet run so the block screamed, and he banged the tiller against the thwart, and he shouted Corin's name once, loudly, toward the right-hand bank, as though looking for a man who had fallen in there. Behind him the oars checked, and a voice said something sharp, and the longboat split its attention for a moment between the boat and the bank.

It was enough to get him into the Heron Creek. It was not enough to get him out of it.

The Heron was narrow and shallow and he had taken it a thousand times at the top of the tide, but this was not the top of the tide and he was not looking where he was going. The Patience hit the bar at the creek's mouth with a long grinding shudder that went up through the keel and into his teeth, and stopped, and heeled, and he was thrown against the thwart so hard that he heard something in his leg go with a sound like a green stick breaking.

He lay in the bilge-water and did not scream, because the longboat was still out there.

After a time — he did not know how long — he heard the oars go past the mouth of the creek, slow now, searching. A lantern swung. A man's voice said, "Nothing. She's gone up the Heron and stuck, she'll be there in the morning, we'll have her then," and another voice, one he thought he knew, said, "And the other one?" and the first voice said, "Drowned, if he's got any sense." Then the oars again, going away, toward the Chapel and the black ship and the salt.

He waited until he could not hear them. Then he dragged himself up onto the thwart, and looked at his leg, and looked away again quickly. The tide was still making. In an hour the Patience would float off the bar. In an hour he would have to be somewhere else.

The tower of the Drowned Chapel was a quarter mile off across the marsh, black against the first grey in the east. It was the only dry place for a mile. It was also where the men in the longboat were going.

Tomas looked at it for a long time. Then he found the boat-hook, and broke the shaft across his knee to make a splint, and began to bind his leg with the sail-ties, and tried to think of something else.

scenes.title: The Boy on the Stair
scenes.text:
Wren found her at the end of the day, as Mother Gannet had promised he would. He was sitting on the Salt House steps when she came out, with the porter glaring at him from the door, and he stood up as soon as he saw her and said, without any greeting at all, "The Patience is up the Heron Creek. Tad Mossop saw her. She's on her side on the bar and there's nobody in her."

Ilse stood on the step with her satchel in her hand.

"Nobody," she said.

"Tad didn't go close. Tad said there was men about. Reeve's men, in a longboat, going up and down." Wren wiped his nose on his cut-down sleeve. "Mother says you'll want to go and look, and Mother says don't, and Mother says if you're going anyway take me, because I know the way at low water and you don't."

"When's low water?"

"Tonight. Middle of the night. It's springs tomorrow, so it'll go right out — you can walk to the Chapel nearly dry-shod if you know where the hard is." He looked at her with an expression that was much older than the rest of his face. "Mother said you'd ask that. Mother said you were your mother's daughter."

She thought about going back up to the third floor and telling the auditor everything. The letter, the sticks, the Kestrel's book in her own hand. She thought about the auditor's kindly hen's face, and about the Reeve's men going up and down the channel in a longboat looking for a boat with her brother in it.

If she told the auditor tonight, the auditor would write to the capital tomorrow, and the capital would send someone in a week. A week was a long time to lie on a bar in the marsh with nobody in your boat.

"I'll need to go home first," she said. "For boots."

"I'll come with you."

"You don't need to."

"Mother said not to let you out of my sight." Wren fell in beside her. "Mother's never wrong. It's very annoying."

They went up Tallow Street together in the dusk, the tall woman in her clerk's grey and the small dirty boy in his enormous coat, and nobody looked at them twice, because that was the kind of street it was. At the cooper's Ilse left Wren on the step and climbed the stair through the middle of the house to her room.

She changed into her mother's old marsh boots, which were too big and which she had kept for ten years without once wearing. She took the letter out of her bodice — it had gone soft with her warmth, the seal tacky — and stood for a moment with it in her hand.

If she went into the marsh with it and they caught her, they would have it. If she left it here —

She put it in the hollow of the bolster, where the sticks had been. Then she took the lamp and went down to Wren.

scenes.title: The Drowned Chapel
scenes.text:
The marsh at low water was a different country. The channels that the Patience had sailed were trickles now, running between banks of mud as high as Ilse's head, and the mud shone in the moonlight like the skin of something sleeping. Wren went ahead of her along a path she could not see — the hard, he called it, a spine of shingle under the mud that the old salt-carriers had used before there were boats — and she followed him step for step and did not look down.

It took them two hours to reach the Chapel. The tower stood up out of the mud on its little island of stone, the arches of the old nave around its foot half-buried, the high windows empty. At high water the sea came in through those windows. Now, with the tide out, there were steps going down into the dark of the crypt, slick with weed, and a smell of salt and old candles.

"Here's where they load," Wren whispered. He pointed. Along the stone of the steps there were fresh scars, white in the moonlight, where something heavy had been dragged. "Salt. Sacks of it. They bring it up the channel from the Pans at night and keep it here dry till the ship comes."

"How do you know?"

Wren shrugged inside his coat. "Everybody knows. Nobody says."

They found Tomas in the tower.

He had dragged himself up the first turn of the stair and wedged himself into a window-niche, and he was so still and so grey that Ilse thought for a long moment that he was dead. Then his eyes opened and he said, quite clearly, "You weren't supposed to come," and she knelt on the stair beside him and held his hand and could not say anything at all.

His leg was splinted with half a boat-hook. He had done it well. He had been sitting in the niche, he said, for a day and a night, while the Reeve's men came and went below him, loading the black ship from the crypt. He had heard everything. He had not been able to move.

"Corin," Ilse said. "Where's Corin?"

"Went over the side. Took them off me." Tomas closed his eyes. "Don't know if he got out. He said to tell you to keep the letter."

"I have it."

"Good. Ilse — listen. The ship's gone. The Black Mare. She went out on this morning's tide with all of it aboard, and she'll be back for the rest." His hand tightened on hers. "And it's not just the Reeve. I heard them. They were talking about the Salt House. About the books. About someone who's going to fix the books before the auditor —"

There was a sound below them. Wren, who had been keeping watch at the foot of the stair, came up it like a cat, silent, his eyes huge.

"Lantern," he breathed. "Two men. On the hard."

They did not move. Ilse put her hand over Tomas's mouth, not because he would have made a sound but because she needed to hold something. Below them, in the ruined nave, a lantern came and went among the arches, and two men came with it, and stood at the head of the crypt steps where the white scars were.

One of them was big and wore a harbour officer's coat. She had seen the Reeve of Varrow at a hundred ceremonies on the quay; she knew his shoulders, his walk, the way he stood with his weight back on his heels.

The other was tall and thin, and held his lantern with a long hand that she had watched sign a thousand pages.

"She's asking for the flood year," the Magister was saying. His voice echoed in the stone. "She's had it on the table for two days. She has copies of the Hesk ledgers, Halvard. Copies. She knew before she came."

"Then she knows nothing she can prove." The Reeve's voice was easy, almost bored. "Hesk ledgers. A clerk in Hesk can't count. Everyone knows that."

"She'll ask for the sticks."

"Then give her the sticks. You told me the sticks were sorted."

The Magister was quiet. The lantern shook a little.

"One of my clerks," he said at last, "found the Kestrel short. Before I could see to it."

"Which clerk?"

Ilse felt Tomas's hand tighten on hers until the bones ground.

"It doesn't matter. I dealt with it. She wrote it in as I told her."

"Oduya." The Reeve sounded almost gentle. "Everything matters. That's how we've lasted three years. Which clerk?"

There was a long silence in the nave. Ilse could hear the water beginning to come back, very far off, a sound like breathing.

"The Varga girl," the Magister said.

scenes.title: The Empty Bolster
scenes.text:
They brought Tomas out on the last of the ebb, the two of them, Ilse under one arm and Wren under the other, and it took four hours, and Ilse did not afterward remember much of it except the cold and the weight and her brother's breath hissing in her ear at every step. Wren found them the hard every time. At the edge of the marsh, where the path came up onto the sea-wall by the Pans, they left Tomas with a pan-man Wren knew, who asked no questions and sent his own son running for a bone-setter, and then Ilse walked home alone through the waking streets with the sun coming up behind her.

The Magister had said her name. She kept hearing it. Not _the clerk_, not _one of my girls_. _The Varga girl_, in that tired voice she had loved for four years, like a man putting down something heavy.

She climbed the stair through the middle of the cooper's house. The step that creaked, creaked. The cooper's wife was not singing.

Her door was open.

Not broken. Open, the way you leave a door when you have a key and are in a hurry. Inside, the room looked almost as she had left it — the table, the chair, the lamp-hook — except that everything had been moved a little and put back a little wrong, the way a stranger puts things back. The chair faced the wrong wall. Her mother's comb was on the left of the shelf instead of the right.

She went back down the stair. The cooper's wife was in the kitchen with the baby on her hip and the door half shut, and when Ilse knocked on it she opened it no wider.

"Was anybody up?" Ilse said. "In the night. To my room."

"I was asleep." The cooper's wife did not look at her. She looked at the baby, who was chewing on a wooden spoon. "We were all asleep. The cooper's been at the Pans all week, you know that, there's nobody here but me."

"My door was open."

"Then you left it open. You were out all night, weren't you? Out in the marsh, by the look of your boots." The woman's eyes went to the boots and came away quickly. "I don't ask where my lodgers go, Miss Varga. I'd thank you not to ask me where I sleep."

"Somebody had a key."

"Then somebody had a key." The cooper's wife began to close the door. "There's three keys to that room and one of them's been lost since Midwinter. Ask the cooper. When he's home."

The door shut. Behind it the baby began to cry, and the woman began to sing to it, the same three lines over and over, too loud.

Ilse stood in the passage for a while. Then she went back up.

Her room was cold. Someone had let the lamp burn down to nothing and the wick had charred, and there was a smell in the air that was not hers — wet wool, and tar, and something sharper, like cloves. She stood in the middle of the floor with her hands at her sides and tried to think the way her mother would have thought. Who had known she was going into the marsh. Who had known she would not be home. Wren had known. Mother Gannet had known. Anyone who had seen her go down Tallow Street at dusk in her mother's boots had known, and half the lower town had.

It did not narrow anything. It only made the room feel larger, and full of people.

The bolster lay on the bed with its seam cut open from end to end.

She did not need to look. She looked anyway. She put her hand into the hollow and felt the feathers and the ticking and nothing else, and then she sat down on the bed with the feathers settling around her like snow, and for the first time since the Kestrel's sticks she let herself cry.

She had not told anyone where she kept it. Not Tomas. Not Wren. Not the auditor, who she had lied to.

She had told no one, and someone had known.

scenes.title: The Magister's Stove
scenes.text:
She went to work. She did not know what else to do with herself, and it seemed important, in a way she could not have explained, that she should be at her place at the long table when the bell went, in her clerk's grey, with her hair pinned, as if nothing had happened. As if she were still the best clerk the Magister had had in thirty years.

Aurek looked up when she came in and opened his mouth to say something about bags of nails, and then looked at her face properly and shut it again.

The auditor was not there. Her sheet of tiny figures lay on the end of the table under a glass paperweight, and the green ledger was gone from beside it.

"She's downstairs," Aurek said quietly. "With him. Since first bell." He hesitated. "Ilse. I took the sticks out of the bin."

She turned.

"The Kestrel's. The night you put them in. I'm not a fool, girl, whatever you think. Nobody finds six sticks behind a stove and then finds them gone again." He did not look at her; he looked at his own ledger, at his own tidy upright hand. "I've been here twenty years. I've written what I was told for three of them. I didn't count. I didn't ask. I told myself the Magister read the margins." He turned a page that did not need turning. "They're in my coat. In the press. If you want them."

She stood very still.

"Why?" she said.

"Because you didn't write anything in the margin," said Aurek Stiles. "You always write in the margin. You've written in the margin every day for four years. And that day you didn't, and I thought: she's frightened. And I thought: I've been frightened for three years and I never once noticed it was the same thing."

At midday the auditor came up the stair and took her sheet of figures from under the paperweight and went down again without a word to either of them. A little after that, the porter came up to say that the Magister wanted Miss Varga in his room.

The stove was lit. It was always lit. Oduya Fenn sat behind his desk with the green ledger closed in front of him and his long hands folded on top of it, and he did not smile when she came in. That was how she knew he had not slept either.

"Sit down, Ilse."

She did not sit down.

"I was at the Chapel last night," she said. "In the tower. With Tomas, who has a broken leg, and has been lying in a window for two days while you loaded salt underneath him."

The Magister closed his eyes.

"I heard you tell the Reeve my name."

"Yes," he said. "I imagine you did." He opened his eyes again and looked at her, and his face was older than she had ever seen it. "Will you let me tell you how it happened? Not to excuse it. I don't think it can be excused. But I'd like someone to know, and I think you've earned it more than anyone."

She sat down.

He told her. The tide in Thawmonth that took the wall and the pans and the pan-reeve's wife. The letter to the capital, and the letter back, _a matter for the harbour._ A whole year of the pan-men sitting on the quay, and the price of salt going up at Hesk, and the Salt House half empty, and the Exchequer writing every quarter to ask why the revenue was down. And then Halvard Seyle in this room, in that chair, with a bottle of something good, saying: _I can build you a wall, Oduya. All it needs is a little salt that nobody counts._

"One part in seven," the Magister said. "For one year. To pay for the wall. That was all it was going to be. I told myself it was the Exchequer's own salt paying for the Exchequer's own wall, and if the Exchequer had done its duty there'd have been no need. I told myself a great many things." He looked down at his hands. "The wall was built in a year. And at the end of the year I went to Halvard and said, that's enough, and he said — he said, Oduya, you've been writing false books for a year. Do you want to explain that to the Exchequer, or shall I?"

"So you kept writing."

"So I kept writing. And the wall is bad stone, and Halvard has a new house, and the Black Mare comes in on the spring tides and takes one-seventh of the salt of Varrow to wherever it goes." He lifted his hands, let them fall. "And you counted the Kestrel's sticks. I knew you would, one day. You're the only one of them who ever counted."

"The letter," she said. "Did you take it?"

His face did not change. "What letter?"

"The Reeve's letter to you. About the Kestrel. I had it."

For a moment the Magister of the Salt House looked at her with an expression she could not read at all, and then, very slowly, he began to laugh. It was not a happy sound.

"He never sent it," he said. "I never had it. I wondered — I wondered why he was so certain I'd been told about the Black Mare coming early, when I hadn't. He said, _I wrote to you._ And I said, _you didn't._ And we each thought the other was lying." He wiped his eyes. "Oh, Ilse. Somebody stole the Reeve's post. And now somebody has stolen it from you."

scenes.title: The Anchor on Rope Walk
scenes.text:
Lisbet Ormund had taken the best room at the Anchor, which was not saying a great deal, and had spent the first evening moving the furniture so that the table caught the light from the window and the bed did not catch the draught from the door. She was at the table now, with her shoes off and her stockinged feet on a hot brick wrapped in flannel, writing her report.

She had written it three times. Each time it said the same thing — _one part in seven, three years, the Salt House books written to conceal it_ — and each time it ended in the same place, which was _I have no proof of who._

When the landlord knocked to say the Reeve was below and wished to call on her, she said, "Yes, of course, send him up," and put her shoes back on, and turned her report face down on the table, and put the hot brick under the bed.

Halvard Seyle filled the doorway. He was a big man and knew it, and he had come in his harbour coat with the gold at the cuffs, and he bowed to her with great courtesy and said he hoped she was comfortable, and that Varrow was not too rough for a lady from the capital, and that if there was anything at all she needed she had only to send to the Reeve's Hall.

"How kind," said Lisbet Ormund. "Do sit down."

He sat. The chair complained.

"I hear you've been at the Salt House books," he said.

"I have."

"Poor Fenn. He's not the man he was. The flood hit him very hard — he took it personally, you know, as though the sea had done it to spite him. I've had to carry a good deal of the work since." He smiled. "If you've found anything amiss, I'd hope you'd come to me first. Before the capital. It would be a shame to ruin an old man's name over a few clerical errors that the harbour could put right quietly."

"A few clerical errors," the auditor repeated.

"Sticks go missing," said the Reeve. "It happens all the time."

Lisbet Ormund looked at him for a long moment with her kindly hen's face. Then she turned her report over on the table and pushed it across to him.

"One part in seven," she said. "Every month for three years. That is not a few clerical errors, Reeve. That is twenty-two thousand crowns of the Exchequer's revenue, near enough, and it is going somewhere, and it is not going to Hesk." She folded her hands. "I'll tell you what I have, since you've been good enough to call. I have the Hesk ledgers. I have the Salt House books. I have a tallyclerk who lied to my face and was frightened to death doing it, and a Magister who hasn't slept in three nights. What I don't have is a name." She smiled at him. "I don't suppose you'd care to give me one?"

The Reeve did not smile back.

"You've been in Varrow four days, madam," he said. "You don't know the tides. People who don't know the tides get into trouble out on the marsh. Every year we lose one or two. Visitors, mostly." He stood up. "I'd be careful."

"I always am," said Lisbet Ormund. "Good night, Reeve."

When he had gone she sat for a while without moving. Then she got the hot brick back out from under the bed, which had gone lukewarm, and put her feet on it, and turned her report face down again, and wrote at the bottom of a fresh sheet, in her tiny neat hand: _Seyle. Certain. No proof._

scenes.title: The Liar Comes Back
scenes.text:
Corin Ashe came back on the night before the spring tide, the way he had come the first time: a knock after midnight, a voice on the landing, a request not to be hit with whatever she was holding.

This time she opened the door all the way.

He looked terrible. He had a cut along his jaw that someone had stitched badly, and his clothes were not his own, and he was thinner than a man ought to get in four days. But he was smiling, and when he saw her face the smile went crooked and then went away altogether.

"Tomas," he said. "Is he —"

"He's alive. His leg's broken. He's at the Pans with a man called Hobb." She stood aside. "Come in. You're letting the cold in."

He came in and stood in the middle of her small room and looked at the bolster, which she had sewn up again, badly, and at the feathers that were still in the corners because she had not been able to bring herself to sweep them.

"I'm sorry about that," he said.

She had known. She had known since the Magister laughed. But she said, "You," anyway, because it needed saying.

"Me." He reached inside his borrowed coat and took out a packet wrapped in oilcloth and held it out to her, exactly as he had on the first night. "Everybody hides things in the bolster, Ilse. I've been in forty rooms in this city. It's always the bolster or the chimney, and you don't have a chimney."

She did not take it. "Why?"

"Because Seyle's men were coming up Tallow Street with a key the cooper's wife had been paid for, and I got there first. Because I knew where they'd look." He was still holding it out. "And because I thought — when I came up out of that creek, half drowned, with the Reeve's men going past me close enough to touch — I thought, I could sell this. I could sell this back to Halvard Seyle for a great deal of money and go to Hesk and never come back. And I had it in my hand on the Hesk road for a whole day before I turned round."

"Why did you turn round?"

He thought about it. She watched him think about it, and was surprised to find that she believed him when he answered.

"Because you didn't hit me with the poker," he said. "The first night. You could have. You had it right there behind the door, I saw the end of it. And you opened the door a hand's width instead, and took a stranger's letter, and kept it." He shrugged. "Nobody's ever done that. Usually they hit me."

She took the letter. The seal was still pressed down where she had warmed it with the knife. He had not opened it again.

"The auditor's at the Anchor," she said. "On Rope Walk."

"I know where the Anchor is."

"Will you come with me?"

Corin Ashe looked at her for a long moment, the long clever face in the lamplight, the scar through his eyebrow.

"I'm a smuggler," he said. "And a liar. Nobody will believe a word I say."

"They'll believe the sticks," said Ilse. "Aurek has the sticks. And they'll believe the letter. And they'll believe me, because I'm going to tell them I lied, and nobody says that unless it's true." She put the letter inside her bodice, against her skin, and reached for her coat. "You only have to stand there."

scenes.title: The Reeve's Hall
scenes.text:
The hearing was called for the hour after noon on the day of the spring tide, in the long hall at the top of the town where the Reeve of Varrow had sat in judgement on fishing disputes and drunk sailors for as long as there had been a Reeve. Lisbet Ormund had called it. She had the right; she had shown the clerk of the Hall a paper with the Exchequer's seal on it, and the clerk had gone white and sent for the Reeve, and the Reeve had come, and smiled, and said that of course the auditor must have whatever she needed.

He sat now in his own chair at the head of the hall, in the harbour coat with the gold at the cuffs. The Magister sat below him on the bench where witnesses sat, very straight, his long hands on his knees. Half the lower town had come up the hill to stand at the back. Ilse could see Mother Gannet's milky eye in the crowd, and Wren's dirty face beside her, and a great many people she had passed on the Gull Stair every day of her life and never spoken to.

The auditor stood at a small table in the middle of the floor with her papers in front of her.

"I'll be brief," she said, "because the tide turns at four and I'm told half of you have boats to see to. I have audited the books of the Salt House of Varrow for the last four years. I find that for the last three of them, one-seventh part of the salt shipped from the Pans has not reached Hesk, and that the books have been written to hide it. I have the Hesk ledgers. I have the Salt House books. Miss Varga."

Ilse stood up.

She had thought her legs would shake. They did not. She walked out to the table in the middle of the floor in her clerk's grey with her hair pinned and laid the things down on it one by one, the way she would have laid out a ship's sticks to be counted.

The Kestrel's book, open at the ninth.

Thirty-four tally-sticks, which Aurek Stiles had brought up the hill in his coat.

A letter with a red seal pressed with a ship under a crown.

"On the ninth," she said, "the Kestrel came in through the Gullet with three hundred and forty measures of salt on her sticks. I wrote four hundred in her book, because I was told to. That was a lie, and it was mine." She heard the crowd at the back shift and murmur. She did not look at them. "Two days later the auditor asked me if I'd ever been told to write a number I knew was wrong, and I said no. That was a lie too."

"Miss Varga," said the Reeve, pleasantly, from his chair. "You'll understand that a clerk who admits to two lies in one breath is not —"

"And this," said Ilse, "is a letter in your hand, Reeve, to the Magister, telling him where the sixty measures from the Kestrel were to go, and when, and on what ship. It never reached him. A man called Corin Ashe took it out of your post-bag, and gave it to me, and I've kept it." She looked up at him. "You can read it, if you like. Or the auditor can read it aloud. It's quite short."

The hall was very quiet.

Halvard Seyle looked at the letter on the table, and at the auditor, and at the Magister on the witnesses' bench, who had not moved. Then he looked past them all to the back of the hall, where Corin Ashe was standing against the wall with his arms folded, in a clean coat, and smiled.

"A smuggler," the Reeve said. "A smuggler steals a letter, and a clerk who lies admits she lies, and an old man —"

"I'll speak to the letter," said Oduya Fenn.

He stood up from the bench. He was not looking at the Reeve; he was looking at Ilse, and his face was quite calm.

"I never received it," he said. "But I know what it says, because I know what every letter Halvard Seyle has written me for three years has said. I'll tell the auditor about every one of them. I'll tell her about the wall. I have kept a book of my own, Madam Auditor — a true one. I kept it because I am a clerk, and I could not bear not to. It is in the stove in my room at the Salt House, behind the firebrick, and it has every measure in it that I ever wrote false."

Somebody in the crowd said, very loudly, "Gods," and somebody else laughed, high and shocked.

The Reeve was on his feet.

"This hearing is closed," he said. "I am the Reeve of Varrow and this is my hall, and I'll not have —"

"It isn't closed, Reeve," said Lisbet Ormund mildly. "It's the Exchequer's hearing. It's only being held in your hall." She picked up the letter. "Sit down, please. I'm going to read this aloud."

He did not sit down. He looked at the auditor, and at the Magister, and at the crowd filling the back of the hall, and something went out of his big red face all at once, like air out of a bladder. Then he turned and walked out through the door behind his chair, the one that only the Reeve used, and nobody stopped him, because nobody in Varrow had ever stopped the Reeve doing anything.

scenes.title: Spring Tide
scenes.text:
The storm came in at four, with the turn of the tide, as the old people on the quay had said it would. It came out of the south-west in one long grey wall, and the sea came with it.

Ilse watched from the top of the Gull Stair. She had run there from the Reeve's Hall with Corin behind her and half the lower town behind him, because Wren had come pelting up the hill shouting that the Reeve's longboat had gone out of the harbour with the Reeve in it, and that the Black Mare was lying off the Chapel again in the teeth of the weather, waiting for him.

"He's mad," Corin said, beside her. He had to shout it. "He'll never get over the bar in this."

"He knows the bar."

"Nobody knows the bar in this."

Out past the harbour mouth the sea had gone white. The salt-ships at their moorings were pitching and snatching at their chains, and the spray was coming over the quay wall in sheets, and down below them on the quay the pilots were out in their oilskins, shouting, hauling boats up the slip. Ilse looked for Tomas among them out of habit before she remembered that Tomas was in a bed at the Pans with his leg in a splint.

Then she saw the longboat.

It was a small dark thing in the white water out by the Chapel, six oars rising and falling out of time, and it was making for the black ship. She could see the Black Mare now too, beyond it — two masts, no sail, her anchors down, plunging. Someone on her deck was waving a light.

"They'll make it," said Corin. "Gods damn him, they'll —"

The sea took the longboat on the Chapel bar.

She did not see it happen. One moment there were six oars and a dark hull and the next there was a wave, enormous, grey-green, standing up across the bar the way the sea stands up only where the bottom is very close, and when it went down there was nothing on the bar but white water. A long way off, the light on the Black Mare's deck stopped waving.

Nobody on the Gull Stair said anything at all.

The Black Mare did not wait. They saw her get her anchors up, or cut them — it was too far to tell — and get a scrap of sail on her, and claw her way round to the south, away from the bar and the Chapel and Varrow. Within half an hour she was gone into the rain.

The Reeve's body came ashore two days later on the hard below the sea-wall at the Pans, the new sea-wall, which had held. One of the pan-men found it. Mother Gannet said afterward that it was the only thing the Reeve ever built that did what it was meant to.

scenes.title: The True Book
scenes.text:
The auditor left Varrow on the twelfth day of Seedmonth, in the same carriage that had come down Tallow Street and frightened the porter, and half the lower town came out to see her go.

She had stayed a fortnight longer than she meant to. She had sat in the Magister's room with the firebrick out of the stove and the Magister's true book open on the desk — a small black book, scorched at the corners, with three years of real numbers in it in a long thin careful hand — and she had copied every page. Then she had sat in the third-floor room with Aurek and Ilse for ten days more and put the real numbers into the real books, page by page, in the margins, in red.

"The Exchequer will want the Magister in the capital," she told Ilse, the last evening, standing at the door of the Salt House with her gloves in her hand. "There'll be a trial. I'll speak for him. I'll say he kept a true book when he could have kept none, and gave it up when he could have burned it, and that's not nothing." She pulled on one glove. "I don't know what they'll do. Something less than they might have, I hope."

"And the Salt House?"

"Will need a Magister." Lisbet Ormund pulled on the other glove. "I've written to say so. I've written to say who." She looked up at Ilse with her kindly hen's face. "Master Stiles has been here twenty years and is a very good clerk, and he told me himself that he would rather go into the sea after the Reeve than have the stove. So I've written your name."

Ilse opened her mouth and shut it again.

"You'll say you're too young," said the auditor. "And that you lied to me. You did. You also told me you'd lied, in front of the whole town, which I have never once in thirty years of this work seen anyone do. Your mother would have." She held out her small gloved hand, and Ilse took it. "Count everything, Miss Varga. Write in the margins. Good night."

The carriage went down Tallow Street in the morning with the carters cursing it, and Ilse watched it from the third-floor window until it was gone.

Tomas came up the Gull Stair that afternoon on two crutches, which took him nearly an hour and which he would not let anyone help him with, and sat on the bench outside the pilots' shed at the bottom with his splinted leg stuck out in front of him and his unlit pipe in his teeth. Corin Ashe sat beside him. Neither of them said much. Corin had a pilot's oilskin on, which was too big for him, and a pilot's book in his pocket, which Tomas had made him buy, and he was learning the Gullet from the bench, channel by channel, with Tomas drawing it in the dust with the end of a crutch.

"He'll make a pilot," Tomas said to Ilse, when she came down to them at the end of the day. "God knows how. He gets everything wrong and then argues with the sea about it."

"I'm very persuasive," said Corin.

"The sea isn't."

Wren was sitting on the bottom step of the Gull Stair eating a cold potato. Mother Gannet was gutting eels. The salt-ships lay over in the mud on the ebb, and the evening light came down the harbour the colour of honey, and somewhere up on the hill a bell was ringing for the end of the day.

Ilse climbed back up to the Salt House as the light went. The third floor was empty; Aurek had gone home. She lit the lamp and sat down at the long table, at her own place, and opened the Kestrel's book at the ninth.

Four hundred, in her own clean hand. And beside it, in the margin, in red, in the auditor's tiny writing: _340. Sticks counted. I.V._

She dipped her pen, and turned to a clean page, and began to count.
